claims.text: The time complexity of binary search is **O(log n)**.
This is because it repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the target with the middle element of the sorted array [3][4].
Binary search needs a sorted array because it depends on the order of elements to eliminate half of the search space at each step.
If the array is unsorted, the middle element might not be the largest or smallest in its half, so the algorithm could skip the target by mistake.
For example, if the middle element is smaller than the target, all elements to its left are also smaller only if the array is sorted [1].
This ensures the algorithm can safely discard the left half [1][2].
Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2` to avoid integer overflow when computing the midpoint [1].
Floyd's tortoise and hare uses two pointers on a linked list: a slow pointer that moves one step at a time and a fast pointer that moves two steps at a time [1].
If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually catch up to the slow pointer inside the cycle, meaning they meet at the same node [1].
If the fast pointer reaches the end (null), there is no cycle [1].
This method works because the fast pointer moves twice as fast, so it will loop around the cycle and meet the slow pointer if one exists.
Inserting at the front of an array is slow (O(n)) because every existing element must shift one position to the right to make space for the new element.
This shifting happens for each insertion, turning a loop of insertions into O(n^2) time [1][2].
To reverse a singly linked list in place, use this method:
Start with `prev = None` and `head` at the list’s start.
Loop through each node:
- Store the `next` node (`nxt = head.next`).
- Reverse the `head.next` pointer to point to `prev`.
- Move `prev` and `head` forward (`prev = head`, `head = nxt`).
When `head` becomes `None`, `prev` is the new head.
This works in **O(n) time** and **O(1) space** by re-pointing nodes [1].
Handle edge cases: empty list (return `None`) and single-node list (return the node) [4].
Appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortized because most of the time, the array has free space, so adding an element takes constant time [2][3].
However, when the array is full, it must resize (copy all elements to a larger block), which takes O(n) time [2].
By doubling the capacity during resizes, the expensive O(n) operations are spread out over many O(1) operations, averaging to O(1) per append [1][2].
Hash tables handle collisions in two main ways:
**Chaining**: Stores colliding keys in a small list at the same bucket.
This keeps all items in one place [1].
**Open addressing**: Finds another free slot in the array (using linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing) to store the colliding item [1].
A good hash function spreads keys evenly to minimize collisions [1].
The load factor of a hash table is calculated by dividing the number of **items** (key-value pairs) by the number of **buckets** in the table [1].
It measures how full the table is.
When this ratio exceeds a set threshold (like 0.75), the table resizes to maintain efficiency [1].
To check balanced brackets with a stack, follow these steps:
Use a stack to track opening brackets (`(`, `[`, `{`).
When you see an opening bracket, push it onto the stack [1].
When you see a closing bracket (`)`, `]`, `}`), check if the stack is empty or if the top of the stack does not match the corresponding opening bracket [1].
If it matches, pop the stack; otherwise, the brackets are unbalanced [1].
After processing all characters, the stack should be empty for the brackets to be balanced [1].
This works because a stack follows LIFO order, ensuring the most recent opening bracket must match the next closing bracket [4].
A monotonic stack solves the next-greater-element problem in O(n) time because each element is pushed and popped **at most once** [1].
As you iterate through the array, you maintain a stack of elements in decreasing order.
When a new element is larger than the top of the stack, it becomes the next greater element for that top element, which is then popped.
This ensures no element stays in the stack longer than necessary, keeping operations efficient.
The process guarantees each element is handled exactly once [1].
A circular buffer is a fixed-size data structure that uses **modulo arithmetic** to wrap around its indices for **head** (front) and **tail** (back) pointers.
It allows **O(1) enqueue and dequeue** operations by reusing empty slots after the tail passes the head.
It avoids shifting elements like a naive array queue [1][2].
Using `list.pop(0)` as a queue is inefficient because it has a time complexity of **O(n)** for each operation, since all remaining elements must shift left [2].
For queues, use `collections.deque` instead, as its `popleft()` operation runs in **O(1)** time [2].
This is why BFS and other queue-based algorithms (like in evidence 3) use `deque` for efficiency [3][4].
A missing or unreachable base case causes infinite recursion, which fills the call stack until it overflows [1].
Each recursive call adds a new frame to the stack, and if recursion never stops, the stack eventually runs out of space [1][4].
Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's **running time or memory usage** grows as the input size (n) increases, focusing on the worst-case scenario [1].
It ignores constant factors and lower-order terms, providing an **upper bound** of growth [1].
For example, O(n) means the time/memory grows at most linearly with input size [1][3].
It does not mean "exactly n steps" or represent the best case [2].
Naive Fibonacci is exponential time (O(2^n)) because it recalculates the same subproblems repeatedly.
For example, to compute `fib(5)`, it calculates `fib(3)` twice, `fib(2)` three times, and so on.
Each call branches into two more calls, leading to a binary tree of computations with roughly 2^n nodes [1][4].
Memoization fixes this by caching results, reducing time to O(n) [2].
Quick sort degrades to **O(n²)** when the pivot selection consistently results in highly unbalanced partitions.
This happens if the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, like in a sorted array with a naive first-element pivot.
Using a random or median-of-three pivot reduces this risk [1].
Worst case is the highest cost for any single input, like a hash table collision causing O(n) time [3].

Amortized cost spreads out occasional expensive operations (like resizing a dynamic array) over many cheap ones, so the *average* per-operation cost is low—like O(1) for appending to a dynamic array [1].
Worst case focuses on a single bad input; amortized cost considers the total cost over many operations.
Insertion sort is best for nearly sorted data because it runs in **O(n)** time when the input is almost sorted.
This is because it only needs to shift elements a little to build the sorted prefix [1].
Merge sort is **stable**—it preserves the relative order of equal elements [2].
It uses **O(n) extra memory** for merging the sorted halves [2].
The code creates temporary arrays (`l`, `r`, `out`) during recursion, requiring space proportional to the input size.

To delete a node with two children in a BST, you replace it with its **inorder successor** (the smallest key in its right subtree) or its **inorder predecessor** (the largest key in its left subtree).
Then, you delete that successor or predecessor node (which will have at most one child) from its original position.
This maintains the BST property [1].
An inorder traversal of a BST gives the node values in **ascending order** (sorted order).
This happens because the BST property ensures all left subtree values are smaller than the current node, and all right subtree values are larger.
The traversal visits left subtree → node → right subtree, producing a sorted sequence [1].

A binary search tree (BST) can degrade to **O(n)** time for operations (search, insert, delete) when it becomes **degenerate**, meaning it turns into a linked list due to unbalanced insertions (e.g., inserting sorted data repeatedly).
This happens because the tree height **h** becomes **n** (like a straight line), making operations linear instead of logarithmic.
The example in evidence shows search takes **O(h)**, which becomes **O(n)** in this case [1].
Preorder traversal visits the **node first**, then its **left subtree**, then its **right subtree** (order: node, left, right) [1].
Inorder traversal visits the **left subtree first**, then the **node**, then the **right subtree** (order: left, node, right) [1].
Postorder traversal visits the **left subtree first**, then the **right subtree**, then the **node** (order: left, right, node) [1].
All three are depth-first traversals, but their order of visiting nodes differs.
For a node at index **i** (0-based) in a heap stored as an array:
- The **left child** index is `2i + 1` [1].
- The **right child** index is `2i + 2` [1].
No pointers are needed because the array layout enforces this structure [1].
A complete binary tree fills every level except possibly the last, which must be filled from left to right.
This means all levels are fully filled until the last one, where nodes are packed to the left as much as possible.
It is also described as a heap structure [1].
The complexity of building a heap from **n** elements using **heapify** is **O(n)**, not **O(n log n)** [1].
This is more efficient than inserting elements one by one (which would be **O(n log n)**).
The heapify process starts from the last non-leaf node and works upward, ensuring the heap property in linear time [1].
Use a size-**k** min-heap to track the top **k** elements efficiently in **O(n log k)** time.
Insert all elements into the heap.
If the heap size exceeds **k**, remove the smallest element (root).
After processing, the heap contains the **k** largest elements.
This works because the min-heap keeps only the **k** largest seen so far at its root [1].
An adjacency list uses **O(V + E)** space, where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges.
It is efficient for sparse graphs (few edges) [1].
An adjacency matrix uses **O(V²)** space, as it stores a V x V table regardless of edges.
It is better for dense graphs (many edges) [1].
BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph by exploring all vertices level by level, starting from the source.
It discovers vertices in order of their distance from the source, ensuring the first time a vertex is reached, it is via the shortest path (fewest edges).
This works because BFS uses a queue to process nodes in the order they are discovered, guaranteeing that closer nodes are processed before farther ones [1].
For weighted graphs, BFS is incorrect—use Dijkstra’s instead [1][4].
Mark nodes **visited when enqueuing** in BFS.
This prevents the same node from being added to the queue multiple times, ensuring efficiency and correctness.
Marking when dequeuing allows duplicates, wasting time and space.

To detect a cycle in a **directed graph** using DFS, you check if DFS reaches a vertex that is **currently on the recursion stack** (a back edge).
This means if you encounter a vertex that is being processed (not fully explored) in the current DFS path, a cycle exists.
Always track vertices on the recursion stack separately from visited vertices [1].
**Pitfall:** Forgetting to reset the recursion stack after finishing a branch can cause false positives [2].
Dijkstra fails with negative edge weights because once a vertex is marked as finalized, its distance is assumed correct.
However, a negative edge later could provide a shorter path to that vertex, making the earlier distance incorrect.
This breaks Dijkstra’s greedy approach of always picking the next closest vertex [1].
For graphs with negative weights, use Bellman-Ford instead, as it can handle them and detect negative cycles [1].
The time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm with a **binary heap** is **O((V + E) log V)**.
This accounts for heap operations (insertions and extractions) across all vertices (V) and edges (E) in the graph [1].
Using topological sorting, a cycle exists if the algorithm does not produce a full ordering (i.e., the length of the returned order is less than the number of vertices).
In Kahn's algorithm, if the final `order` list has fewer than `n` nodes, it means some nodes were never processed due to cyclic dependencies, indicating a cycle [4].
This works because a topological order only exists in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) [2].
Kahn's algorithm uses in-degree to track how many edges point to each vertex.
It starts by enqueuing all vertices with an in-degree of 0, meaning no edges lead into them [1].
As it processes each vertex, it removes it from the graph (conceptually) by decrementing the in-degree of its neighbors.
If a neighbor's in-degree reaches 0, it means all its dependencies have been processed, so it is enqueued [1].
This ensures vertices are only processed once all their prerequisites are done.
Path compression flattens the tree during a `find` operation by making every node point directly to its root, reducing future lookup times.
It’s done in the `find` method by updating `self.p[x] = self.p[self.p[x]]` before moving up the tree [1].
Union by rank (or size) attaches the smaller tree under the larger one during a `union` to keep the tree balanced.
In the code, it compares `self.size[ra]` and `self.size[rb]` to decide which root becomes the parent [1].
This ensures operations stay efficient.
The inverse Ackermann function, **alpha(n)**, in Union-Find complexity measures how quickly the tree height grows with optimizations.
With **path compression** and **union by size/rank**, the tree height remains extremely small—effectively constant for practical purposes.
The inverse Ackermann function grows so slowly that **alpha(n) ≤ 4** for all computable values of *n* [1].
This means each **find** or **union** operation is nearly **O(1)** in practice [1].
